explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for statements throughout the procedure.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some runtime errors can leave the later explicit transaction open.
@CustomerIdText fixes the customer lookup to ID 1 rather than using the supplied customer ID.
@OrderID starts at the specific business identifier 1, which is used in an order lookup before reassignment.
Returning every Orders column includes large text fields and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
No ordering determines which ten order IDs are returned.
OrderID is the Orders primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any rows.
NOLOCK can return uncommitted order IDs or miss rows during concurrent writes.
YEAR(OrderDate) prevents the year filter from being used directly as a date range.
The reporting year is fixed at 2016 rather than supplied as a filter.
Comparing integer CustomerID to nvarchar @CustomerIdText requires converting the text to int.
The same predicate must support both an unrestricted scan and an indexed CustomerID lookup.
The initial % in '%urgent%' requires searching within Comments rather than matching a prefix.
ISNULL wraps indexed CustomerID even though the column is NOT NULL and needs no fallback.
The predicate selects customer ID 1 rather than using @CustomerID.
Adding zero to OrderID obscures a direct equality lookup on the primary key.
Excluding one CustomerID can require reading most of Orders.
The excluded customer is fixed to ID 1.
TOP (1) chooses an unspecified order/customer pair.
The cross join allows an order to be paired with a customer other than its own.
No ordering determines which matching order line supplies the returned OrderID.
The comma join separates the Orders-OrderLines relationship from its table declarations.
LineCount is expressed as a separate correlated count for each order, which can lead to repeated OrderLines lookups.
The existence test correlates qualifying lines by OrderID. SQL Server can implement this as a semi-join; a plain inner join could duplicate orders.
The qualifying line-quantity threshold is fixed at 1.
ORDER BY repeats the CASE expression already named HasComments, so the two definitions can drift.
ORDER BY 2 silently changes meaning if OrderDate moves in the select list.
Orders with equal OrderDate have no defined relative order, so page membership can change without a unique tie-breaker.
The branches select different primary-key values, so UNION does not need to eliminate duplicates.
The first branch embeds order ID 1.
The second branch embeds order ID 2.
Only the presence of a matching order line matters; the exact line count is unused.
All orders qualify to assign @OrderID, leaving its final value dependent on an unspecified processing order.
The five IDs inserted into @OrderIds are not selected in a defined order.
SELECT INTO implicitly derives the #ImplicitOrders schema from the projection.
No ordering determines which five orders populate #ImplicitOrders.
A cursor is allocated and opened just to fetch one OrderID before it is closed.
Embedding the converted @CustomerID produces different SQL text for different customers; a NULL input also nulls the batch text.
EXEC runs the constructed customer lookup without binding @CustomerID.
Converting @OrderID to text embeds the value in a new query string instead of keeping the statement reusable.
sys.sp_executesql receives only SQL text, not an integer parameter for the order lookup.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped, retaining the unused object until procedure exit.
Returning IgnoredError as a result row does not signal failure or stop subsequent statements.
The negative-order-ID error uses legacy RAISERROR rather than THROW.
PRINT emits a buffered, unstructured diagnostic rather than a reliable status signal.
The Orders lookup fixes CustomerID at 1 despite the available @CustomerID parameter.
The order cutoff '20160101' is embedded without a named business meaning.
Without an explicit style, '01/02/2016' can mean January 2 or February 1 depending on DATEFORMAT.
No ordering determines which joined order is returned.
COALESCE wraps o.CustomerID unnecessarily: Orders.CustomerID is NOT NULL and can be joined directly.
COALESCE also wraps i.CustomerID, obscuring the indexed invoice join key despite its NOT NULL constraint.
TOP (1) returns an unspecified order ID from the self-join.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key contributes neither another value nor a filter.
Sorting by nvarchar(max) Comments can require large comparisons and spill sort data to tempdb.
SUM(Quantity) reads quantities across the entire OrderLines table.
OrderID > 0 depends only on the grouping key and can filter source rows in WHERE.
COUNT(*) requests an exact count across all of Orders without a restrictive predicate.
The ungrouped count returns one row, so sorting by OrderCount cannot affect the result.
MERGE adds matching machinery for a single update branch with no insert or delete action.
The matched branch writes target.Comments back to itself and can fire update triggers without changing the value.
Assigning Comments to itself can acquire write locks and trigger update handling without changing the order.
Quantity alone can match lines from unrelated orders, deleting all of them when writes are enabled.
The delete treats quantity -1 as a deletion marker without naming or validating that business convention.
WAITFOR deliberately holds the request open for one second.
The transaction begins outside TRY/CATCH, with no error-handling path covering it before the rollback.
Sales.Orders has no IDENTITY column in the supplied schema, so enabling IDENTITY_INSERT fails if this branch runs.
sp_who is invoked without its sys schema qualifier.
ROWCOUNT remains 1 for the rest of the procedure, silently limiting later queries and the insert into #DemoCustomers.
The category ID and name are assigned by physical column position rather than by an explicit target list.
Every new demo category is assigned the fixed category ID 99.
The four projected customer values depend on the declaration order of #DemoCustomers columns.
The initial % prevents a prefix seek on the unique CustomerName index.
@CustomerName is inserted into a quoted SQL literal, allowing input to change the executed statement. Bind the search pattern as a parameter.
sp_executesql executes the name-search batch without a parameter declaration or a bound search value.
The dynamic execution routine is called as sp_executesql rather than sys.sp_executesql.
No predicate identifies which demo customer should receive the category change; ROWCOUNT is not a customer-selection criterion.
CustomerCategoryID is set to the fixed business identifier 1.
The WHERE predicate rejects NULL-extended order rows, excluding customers without a qualifying order despite the LEFT JOIN.
The order-date cutoff '2016-01-01' is fixed directly in the customer query.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL cannot evaluate to true under ANSI NULL semantics; the column is also declared NOT NULL.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) can incur a scalar function invocation per customer unless SQL Server inlines it.
The transaction handler returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as data and continues without reporting failure to the caller.
An error after BEGIN TRANSACTION can bypass COMMIT, and the handler does not roll back an outstanding transaction.
INDEX = 1 forces the clustered index on Customers, excluding the CustomerName index even for a selective prefix search.
Three nested derived tables merely pass CustomerID through; the filter and projection need only one query.
The initial % in '%A%' prevents a prefix seek on CustomerName.
The result exposes every column of GetCustomerOrdersMulti and changes if the function's return schema changes.
If GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF as its name suggests, its result table can limit optimization. Its definition is needed to confirm whether it can be rewritten inline.
